title: "But Allah"
hookLine: then a yes: only Allah is worshiped

cards: What do you do with a cleared room? Empty a closet or a garage, and there comes a moment: the junk is gone, the floor is bare, and there's a strange quiet.
Leave it empty long enough and it fills back up with whatever wanders in. The shahadah doesn't leave the room empty. Right after the no comes one short word, illa, but, except.
And after it, the one name it was clearing the room for.

teach.b: La ilaha illallah. No god but Allah. First, the hinge: illa.
It means but, or except. The sentence is built as a no to everything, then one exception. So it doesn't just say Allah is a god.
It says nothing else is to be worshiped, only Allah. The no and the yes make one claim. Second, who the yes is for.
The verse Muslims know as the Throne Verse opens, in Pickthall's translation: "Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive, the Eternal." The Alive, where yesterday's stars set and went dark.
The Eternal, where everything that rises comes down again. The yes goes to the one thing that doesn't set. Third, what the yes does inside a person.
The Qur'an says, in Pickthall: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!" The cleared room isn't left cold. Something lives there now, and the verse calls the result rest.
La ilaha illallah is short, and its sounds roll into one another, so it can be said under the breath while walking, cooking, or lying awake.

A hadith in Tirmidhi's collection calls it the best remembrance, and some Sufi circles repeat it together, sometimes with the rhythm of the breath. In a crowd or alone in a car, the shape is the same: first no, then yes.

how: Muslims repeat la ilaha illallah as dhikr, remembrance, after prayers, on prayer beads, or quietly through the day; some Sufi circles say it together, sometimes in time with the breath.

o: a hope that God will forgive whatever came before
the yes after the no: only Allah is to be worshiped
a claim that Allah is the greatest of many gods

s: la ilaha illallah only says that Allah is a god
it's a no to everything and one exception: none is to be worshiped but Allah.
the Throne Verse calls Allah the Alive, the Eternal
"Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive, the Eternal."
la ilaha illallah can only be said in the formal prayer
it's said as remembrance anywhere: walking, cooking, lying awake.

games.q: you've cleared a room of everything that didn't belong. the shahadah has said its no. what comes next?
o: let a few old things back in.
games.why: illallah: the sentence never leaves the room empty. the no exists to make space for the yes.

practice: Let your breathing find its own pace.

If you pray, say la ilaha quietly as you breathe out, letting go, and illallah as you breathe in, letting the yes fill the space; if you'd rather not say the words, just feel the shape: out, clear the room; in, let something good fill it.
No counting, only the two halves, as slowly as the breath wants.

wordCard.voice: But Allah. Illallah: the yes after the no, the one exception the whole sentence was built to hold. Today's word.

orig.note: but Allah: the second half of la ilaha illallah, where illa means except.

carryVoice: Your line: then, yes. The cleared room doesn't stay empty. Back tomorrow, same hill.
